passage: Baljeet, you ask why your Bua Yamini never shouts? Because I once shouted so loud my own father stopped talking to me for three days. I was sixteen. A friend's cousin was having a sangeet in the next colony, ending at eleven. Papa said no. I said, "Everyone is going! Everyone's parents allow it! You are the strictest father in the world!" I slammed the door so hard the photograph fell. Papa's jaw tightened. "Then everyone's parents can look after everyone," he said. "My answer is no, and it will be no next time also." Mummy tried to soften it, but Papa raised a hand. I sat in my room crying, sure I had been right. Yet I had not asked him one question. I had only given orders.

qa.q: What time was the sangeet due to end?
qa.a: The sangeet was due to end at eleven.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when slamming the door, and what shows it?
qa.a: Yamini was angry, hurt and sure of being right; the shouting and the slammed door show it.

qa.q: What could Yamini have tried instead of shouting, and why?
qa.a: Yamini could have asked what worried Papa and offered a plan such as a ride home, because shouting made Papa dig in while a question would have opened a talk.

qa.q: How did Papa see the shouting?
qa.a: Papa likely saw a challenge to his authority and not a real request, so he held firm and refused even for next time.

grounding: The teen shouts that everyone else is allowed and that parents are too strict, the argument becomes a power struggle, and the request is refused outright.

passage: The concert started at seven, it was already five, and Baljeet still didn't have permission. He found his parents in the kitchen, both tired after a long day at the shop. "I'm going to the concert tonight with Harjot and them." "Where is it? Who's driving? When does it end?" Mummy asked. "Why does it matter? Everyone else is allowed! You're the strictest parents in the whole school!" Papa put down his cup. "Don't shout in this house." "I'm not shouting!" he shouted. His sister Ritu, doing homework at the table, slowly slid her books out of the room. Each question from Mummy got a louder answer. By a quarter to six Papa said, very quietly, "No. Not tonight. And we'll talk about next month's trip too." Baljeet slammed his door. Harjot's texts kept coming: "where r u??"

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling in the kitchen?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and panicky with time running out, and it came out as angry shouting.

qa.q: What could Baljeet have done differently at five?
qa.a: Answered Mummy's questions calmly with details about the venue, transport and end time, since she was asking for information, not refusing.

qa.q: What was the scene like for Ritu?
qa.a: Ritu seemed uncomfortable, quietly sliding her books out of the room to escape the shouting.

grounding: Shows a teen under time pressure shouting that everyone else is allowed, turning the talk into a power struggle and getting a flat refusal.

passage: Trisha had rehearsed it in the lift, but by the time she reached the flat in Hyderabad the plan was gone. "Everyone is going to Ritika's farmhouse sleepover. Everyone. Why am I the only one who's never allowed anything?" Her mother, Kavitha, kept chopping onions. "Whose farmhouse? Will her parents be there?" "Oh my God, you don't trust me! Do you know how embarrassing you are?" Kavitha put the knife down. "I asked a question." "You always ask questions! Other parents just say yes!" Now her mother's voice went flat. "Then the answer is no." "That's so unfair!" "And the school trip next month, we'll see." Trisha stormed to her room. Lying face down on the bed, she realised she still didn't know whether Ritika's parents would even be there.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel lying on her bed?
qa.a: She felt angry and humiliated, and a bit foolish, realising she didn't even know whether Ritika's parents would be there.

qa.q: What would have worked better than saying everyone is going?
qa.a: Answering her mother's questions calmly, finding out whether Ritika's parents would be there, and giving details so the request could be weighed.

qa.q: How did Kavitha seem to feel as the argument grew?
qa.a: She seemed hurt and then firm, her voice going flat as the shouting turned it into a power struggle.

grounding: Shows a teen demanding permission and calling her mother too strict, so the talk becomes a power struggle and the request is refused.
